name: Razor strop

lead: A razor strop is a flexible strip, classically leather, that straightens and polishes the edge of a straight razor. A well-maintained edge gives a smoother, closer shave and cleaner beard lines.
Strops come as hanging straps, table or hand-held blocks and paddles, and can carry fine abrasive compounds for a mirror-like edge.

paras: Straight razor shavers draw the blade along the strop before shaving as routine edge maintenance. Leather is the classic surface, with canvas, denim or balsa wood also used, and abrasive pastes added by some users.
Straight razors are open blades and cuts are possible during shaving. Stropping a blade badly can also damage the edge.

angle.text: A stropped edge cuts cleanly, which straight-razor users link to close shaves and precise beard outlines.

lead: A razor strop is a flexible strip of soft material, typically leather, used to straighten and polish a blade. It is most associated with straight razors, the thinnest blades in everyday use, which need frequent stropping.[1]

For grooming, a well-kept edge is what makes straight-razor shaving possible, and forum posts about wet shaving describe it as a route to a very close shave and precise beard lines.[2][3] Stropping realigns an edge that has been bent out of line, and with an abrasive compound it can remove a small amount of metal and burnish the blade.[1]

Strops come as hanging straps, blocks that sit on a table or are held in hand, and hand-held paddles. Materials include leather, canvas, denim and balsa wood, with abrasives such as diamond, chromium oxide, aluminum oxide or iron oxide added to some.[1]
infobox: Diamond, chromium oxide, aluminum oxide, iron oxide[1]

paras: Hanging straps are the traditional form; blocks and paddles are used on a bench or in hand.[1] Custom strops exist for irregular tools such as chisels and gouges, and in principle any blade can be stropped.[1]

T Nation forum members discussing straight razors describe the strop as the maintenance step that keeps the razor sharp. One poster listed it as the main extra cost beyond the razor, while another said the full kit of brush, soap and strop made it too much hassle.[2][3] One shaver reported never getting a closer shave than with a straight razor.[4]
